turns.text:
Back in August I asked my ex if we could swap Thanksgiving this year. My mom turns 70 that week and my family is meeting in Honolulu. I offered him Christmas Eve and Christmas Day in exchange. He wrote back "Probably fine." I said thank you, I'd start looking at flights. He didn't object. Not a word about it for two months.

So in September I booked three tickets, me and our two kids. $2,640, nonrefundable. Then on October 14 he texts that his dad had surgery, he needs the kids for Thanksgiving, and he can't do the swap. I told him I'd already booked. His answer was "I said probably." I called him twice that night. He didn't pick up. At 7:30 the next morning he emails me with our mediator copied, quoting the plan at me. Now he's treating it like a court case. He never said no until I'd paid for it.

I'm sorry about his dad, I really am. But I think he's using it to get back at me for leaving. My mom only turns 70 once. I'm gutted, and I don't know what to tell the kids.

Am I wrong to hold him to the swap?

You are completely justified in feeling gutted and furious. You gave him a heads-up, he gave you a soft green light, and you explicitly told him you were moving forward with flights. To pull the rug out from under you two months later—after the money is spent and the excitement is built—feels incredibly unfair.

However, looking at this purely through a co-parenting and legal lens, **you will likely have a very hard time holding him to the swap.** As maddening as it is, "probably fine" is not a definitive, documented agreement. Now that he has looped in the mediator and anchored himself to the official parenting plan, the default will almost certainly revert to the court-ordered schedule. Add in his father’s surgery, and he has a heavily defensible reason on paper to deny the change, regardless of whether you suspect he is weaponizing it to punish you.

Fighting this through the mediator will likely drain your energy and wallet without getting you on that flight to Honolulu. Instead, it might be best to pivot to damage control and protect your peace.

**Call the airline directly.** Explain that a sudden family medical emergency and custody change forces you to cancel the kids' tickets. Even "nonrefundable" fares can sometimes be converted into future travel credits for the passengers if you get a sympathetic agent on the phone.

**Keep the mediator communication strictly business.** Take the high road to protect your image in the mediation record. You can state calmly: "Based on our August conversation where I explicitly mentioned booking flights, I proceeded with the purchase. However, I understand your father had surgery and you are now enforcing the default holiday schedule. I am disappointed this change wasn't communicated before October, but the kids will be with you for Thanksgiving." This leaves a clear paper trail of your reasonable behavior and his poor communication.

**Address the kids neutrally.** Keep it brief to shield them from the conflict. Something like: "Grandpa had surgery, so Dad really needs you with his family for Thanksgiving this year. We won't make it to Hawaii, but we are going to plan our own amazing way to celebrate Grandma's birthday."

Does your parenting plan happen to contain any clauses about how financial losses are handled when informal agreements or travel plans fall through?

You are absolutely right that his communication was terrible and it was deeply unfair to let you believe this trip was happening. In the normal world of human relationships, "probably fine" followed by two months of silence after you explicitly said you were booking tickets means yes. **You have every right to feel completely wronged.**

But in the rigid world of post-divorce co-parenting, booking a $2,600 non-refundable trip without a documented, definitive "yes" was a risk. **He is hiding behind the technicality of the parenting plan, and unfortunately, the legal framework allows him to do exactly that.**

So morally and interpersonally? You are entirely in the right. Legally and practically? He found a loophole and used it.
